title: SRE SLOs, Error Budgets, Capacity Planning, Reliability Initiatives, and Runbooks
author: Ari Chen
body:
Overview:
This document consolidates Redwood Inference SRE guidance for defining and operating service-level objectives (SLOs) and error budgets, capacity planning and autoscaling policies, reliability initiatives, incident review standards, operational tooling, and canonical runbook templates. It is intended for service owners, SREs, and platform engineers who run production inference services across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments.

Goals:
- Provide a consistent SLO taxonomy and error budget lifecycle for all externally observable services.
- Standardize capacity planning and autoscaling guardrails to meet latency SLOs while controlling cost.
- Define incident review and postmortem standards for measurable learning and corrective action.
- Catalog operational tooling and runbook templates so responders have a single source of truth.

Scope and applicability:
- Applies to all externally customer-facing inference services, control-plane components, and tier-1 internal services (scheduling, routing, billing API).
- Tiering: tier-1 (user-facing request path), tier-2 (supporting infrastructure), tier-3 (internal tooling). Different SLO targets and review cadence apply by tier.

1) SLOs and Error Budgets

Principles:
- Define SLOs on user-observable indicators (latency, availability, model correctness where measurable).
- Keep SLOs simple and actionable: one objective per SLO.
- Align error budgets with rollout and change control processes.

Standard SLO types and examples:
- Availability SLO (requests succeeding end-to-end): "p99 success rate >= 99.95% over a 30-day rolling window" for tier-1 endpoints.
- Latency SLO (end-to-end request latency): "p95 latency < 200ms for text-generation (short prompts) over 7-day rolling window".
- Throughput SLO (capacity): "95th percentile throughput >= reserved capacity for Dedicated pools over 7-day window".
- Quality guardrail (model-level): "No more than 1.0% regression on critical eval dataset A over a 14-day rolling window after model rollout".

SLO definitions should include the following fields (SLO metadata):
- owner (team), metric name, window (7d/30d/90d), target, measurement method, instrumentation (metric source), alert thresholds, linked runbook, and escalation path.

Error budget policy:
- Error budget = 1 - SLO target. Example: 99.95% SLO => error budget = 0.05% of requests in window.
- Burn rate monitoring: set burn-rate alerts: soft (2x burn rate for 6 hours), critical (4x burn rate for 1 hour) depending on window.
- Operational responses by burn state:
  - Healthy: normal change/rollout cadence.
  - At-risk (soft alert): Halt low-priority rollouts, reduce aggressive autoscaling or batch sizes, increase observability sampling.
  - Exhausted (critical alert): Pause all non-essential releases, escalate to incident review and on-call manager, run rollback or mitigation steps.

Integration with rollouts and CI/CD:
- Every canary/rollout must declare the SLO(s) it may impact and the rollback criteria tied to error budget burn.
- Automated gating: if error budget burn crosses critical during rollout, CI/CD must automatically pause or rollback the rollout.

2) Capacity Planning and Autoscaling

Capacity planning goals:
- Meet latency and availability SLOs at 99th% traffic patterns while minimizing over-provisioning.
- Account for tail latencies, model sequence length variability, and peak traffic patterns (day-of-week, seasonal).

Forecasting process (quarterly + ad-hoc before major releases):
1. Collect telemetry (QPS, token/sec, p95/p99 latency, sequence length histogram) for the last 90 days.
2. Identify growth rate (baseline week-over-week and event-driven spikes).
3. Model capacity needs: plan for N% buffer (default 25%) above predicted 99th percentile traffic for tier-1 endpoints.
4. Validate with load tests (synthetic and replay) on staging Dedicated pools.
5. Schedule capacity acquisition (cloud/GPU reservations) 30-60 days ahead of projected peak.

Autoscaling policy template:
- Scale metric: target = p95 latency; horizontal autoscale on CPU/gpu utilization + queue length; vertical scaling for host-level resource changes.
- Minimum capacity: reserved pool sized for 95th percentile baseline for Dedicated customers.
- Cooldown: 2 minutes for scale-up, 5-10 minutes for scale-down for batching-sensitive workloads.
- Burst bucket: transient burst headroom (15-30% of pool) to be consumed before on-demand provisioning.

Capacity guardrails table (text representation):
- "metric_thresholds": ["gpu_utilization >= 75% -> trigger scale-up policy","request_queue_length >= 100 -> increase replicas by ceil(queue_length / 50)","p95_latency > target for 3 consecutive 1m windows -> trigger emergency autoscale + alert"]

3) Reliability Initiatives and SRE Programs

Program types and cadence:
- Preventative: quarterly reliability reviews and chaos engineering exercises on non-customer-critical paths.
- Progressive: reliability improvement OKRs per quarter tied to measurable SLO improvements.
- Reactive: incident-driven corrective action plans and blameless postmortems.

Example initiatives (past and planned):
- Prefix/KV cache improvements that reduced p99 tail latency for long-context models by 18% (Q1 2026).
- Enhanced kernel selection heuristics to avoid hot-path stalls under variable seq-lens (planned Q2 2026).
- Introduce model-level shadow testing pipeline to detect quality regressions earlier (planned).

Measuring program success:
- Delta in aggregate error budget burn across tier-1 services quarter-over-quarter.
- Reduction in mean time to recover (MTTR) for cache-related incidents by 30% within two quarters.

4) Incident Review Standards and Postmortems

Incident severity taxonomy (example):
- Sev 1: Major service outage affecting >10% of customers or >50% of requests for >5 minutes.
- Sev 2: Significant degradation affecting important customers/paths but partial availability.
- Sev 3: Minor degradation or single-customer impact.

Incident review process (required for Sev1/Sev2 within 72 hours):
1. Create a canonical incident page with timeline, alerts, runbook steps executed, mitigations, and owner.
2. Collect key telemetry: error budget burn, CPU/GPU utilization, queue lengths, latency percentiles, sample traces, and impacted model variants.
3. Conduct blameless postmortem within 7 business days. Postmortem must include: summary, impact, timeline, root cause analysis (RCA), corrective actions (short/medium/long term), owner(s), and due dates.
4. Track action items in a central tracker and review closure monthly in reliability review forum.

Postmortem quality checklist:
- Was the RCA specific and evidence-backed?
- Are action items small, time-boxed, and assigned?
- Is the follow-up tracked to closure with metrics?

5) Operational Tooling and Observability

Required observability signals:
- Request-level: request id, user/customer id (hashed), model id/version, route, latency (p50/p95/p99), success/failure, error type, KV cache hit/miss, token counts.
- Host-level: GPU utilization, allocator stalls, memory pressure, process restarts, kernel-level stalls.
- Platform-level: queue lengths, autoscaler decisions, cluster-level utilization, network egress/inbound errors.

Dashboards and alerts (minimum set):
- SLO dashboard: current window SLO attainment, burn rate, and historical trend.
- Latency heatmap: by route and model variant.
- Capacity dashboard: pod/node utilization, queue lengths, and pending scale ops.
- Incident triage panel: top error types, top affected customers, and recent deploys.

Tooling integrations and playbooks:
- PagerDuty for on-call notifications (severity mappings and escalation policy).
- Slack incident channels auto-created by incident service with pinned runbook link.
- Automated runbook runner (CLI tool: rrun) to capture steps executed and tag telemetry for postmortem. Example usage:
  - rrun start --incident-id INC-2026-1234 --runbook inference-rebuild-cache
  - rrun step "restart serving pool" --cmd "kubectl rollout restart deployment/inference-serving"

6) Canonical Runbook Templates

Each runbook must be short, actionable, and have clear pre-reqs, detection, mitigation, and recovery steps. Reference template fields (must be present in every runbook):
- runbook_id (short slug), title, service, owner_oncall_role, severity, detection_signals, preconditions, safe-mitigation-steps, recovery-steps, verification-steps, rollback-criteria, post-incident-actions.

Example runbook: inference-high-latency-short-prompts
- service: inference-serving
- owner_oncall_role: inference-oncall (primary)
- severity: Sev2 -> escalate to Sev1 if >30% requests impacted for 10+ minutes
- detection_signals: p95 latency > 200ms for 3 consecutive 1m windows; queue_length > 100
- preconditions: recent deploy within last 60 minutes? yes/no (flag)
- safe-mitigation-steps:
  1) Check autoscaler: `kubectl get hpa -n inference` and verify scale ops.
  2) Increase replica count by +2: `kubectl scale deploy inference-serving --replicas=$(($(kubectl get deploy inference-serving -o jsonpath='{.spec.replicas}')+2))`
  3) If using Dedicated: hot-add GPU nodes via capacity manager UI and pin traffic away from degraded pool.
- recovery-steps:
  1) If mitigation reduces p95 below target for 10 minutes, run gradual rollback of temporary scale changes.
  2) If degraded due to model variant, rollback to previous model version per model-rollout SOP.
- verification-steps:
  1) Monitor SLO dashboard and traces for 30 minutes.
  2) Validate sample responses for correctness and latency.

Runbook maintenance and ownership:
- Owners must review runbooks quarterly and after any related incident.
- Runbooks must include last-reviewed date and owner contact (rotating on-call role acceptable).

7) Ownership, Governance and Next Steps

- SLO owners: every SLO must have a single team owner and a documented secondary.
- Review cadence: SLO calibration quarterly; reliability program review monthly.
- Automation: implement error-budget gating in CI/CD pipelines for all canaries by end of Q2 2026.
- Playbook adoption: require that every tier-1 service has an authored runbook and SLO before production access is granted to new teams.

Appendix A: Example SLO JSON (measurement example)
{
  "slo_id": "inference-p99-success-30d",
  "service": "inference-serving",
  "metric": "request_success",
  "window": "30d",
  "target": "0.9995",
  "owner": "inference-platform",
  "measurement_source": "prometheus:service_request_success_ratio"
}

Appendix B: Quick runbook checklist for on-call responders:
- Verify alert context and recent deploys.
- Confirm scope (single-customer vs global).
- Execute safe mitigations from canonical runbook.
- Annotate all steps with rrun.
- If error budget is burning fast, escalate to on-call manager and follow emergency rollback play.
